'''Sir David Klenerman''' (born 1959) is a British [[Biophysical chemistry|biophysical chemist]] and a professor of biophysical chemistry at the [[Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|Department of Chemistry]] at the [[University of Cambridge]]<ref name="Faculty Webpage">{{cite web|title=Professor David Klenerman FMedSci FRS|url=https://www.ch.cam.ac.uk/person/dk10012|website=Department of Chemistry, University of Cambridge|publisher=[[University of Cambridge]]|access-date=26 January 2016}}</ref> and a [[Fellow]] of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]].<ref name="Christ Profile">{{cite web|title=Professor David Klenerman|url=https://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/content/professor-david-klenerman|publisher=[[Christ's College, Cambridge]]|access-date=26 January 2016}}</ref>

He is best known for his contribution in the field of [[next-generation sequencing]] of DNA (that subsequently resulted in [[Solexa]], a high-speed DNA sequencing company that he co-founded),<ref name=ch/><ref name="Illumina History">{{cite web|title=History of Illumina Sequencing|url=https://www.illumina.com/technology/next-generation-sequencing/solexa-technology.html|publisher=[[Illumina ==Early life and education==
Klenerman is the son of two South African-born Jews.<ref name="Frazer">{{cite news |last1=Frazer |first1=Jenni |title=Seven Holocaust survivors on New Year's Honours List |url=https://www.jewishnews.co.uk/six-holocaust-survivors-on-new-years-honours-list/ |access-date=14 February 2024 |work=[[Jewish News]] |date=2018-12-28}}</ref> He was educated at the [[University of Cambridge]] where he was an undergraduate student of [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] and received his [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] degree in 1982.<ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Klenerman, Prof. David | id = U266724 | year = 2017 | doi =10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.266724 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> He earned his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] degree in chemistry in 1986 as a postgraduate student of [[Churchill College, Cambridge]] and was supervised by [[Ian William Murison Smith]].<ref name=kphd>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Cambridge|url=http://idiscover.lib.cam.ac.uk/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=44CAM_ALMA21428177930003606&context=L&vid=44CAM_PROD&search_scope=SCOP_CAM_ALL&tab=cam_lib_coll&lang=en_US|title=Infrared chemiluminescence using a SISAM spectrometer|first= David|last=Klenerman|date=1985|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.355881}}|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|oclc=499899771}}</ref><ref name="RSC Award" /><ref name=whoswho />

==Career and research==
After his doctorate, Klenerman went to [[Stanford University]] as a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright scholar]] to work on high-overtone chemistry, with [[Richard Zare]]. After his [[postdoctoral research]] at Stanford, he returned to United Kingdom to work in [[BP]] Research for seven years. Then, in 1994, he joined the University of Cambridge, as a faculty member of the Department of Chemistry and a fellow of Christ's College.<ref name="RSC Award" /><ref name=whoswho /><ref name=christfrs>{{cite web|title=David Klenerman elected FRS|url=https://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/default/news/david-klenerman-elected-frs|publisher=[[Christ's College, Cambridge]]|access-date=27 January 2016|archive-date=25 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825150633/https://www.christs.cam.ac.uk/default/news/david-klenerman-elected-frs}}</ref>

Klenerman, along with [[Shankar Balasubramanian]], invented a method of next-generation [[DNA sequencing]] which is commonly known today as the Solexa sequencing or [[Illumina dye sequencing]].<ref name="Illumina History" /><ref name=Nature /> The method is based on the detection of [[fluorophore]] labelled nucleotides as they get incorporated in the [[DNA]] strands.<ref name="Chem Comm">{{cite journal|last1=Balasubramanian|first1=Shankar|title=Sequencing nucleic acids: from chemistry to medicine|journal=[[Chemical Communications]]|date=4 May 2011|volume=47|issue=26|pages=7281–7286|doi=10.1039/c1cc11078k|pmid=21544287|pmc=3428630}}</ref> This sequencing by synthesis method gained popularity,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Quail|first1=Michael A|title=A large genome center's improvements to the Illumina sequencing system|journal=[[Nature Methods]]|date=25 November 2008|volume=5|issue=12|pages=1005–1010|doi=10.1038/nmeth.1270|pmid=19034268|pmc=2610436}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cronn|first1=Richard|title=Multiplex sequencing of plant chloroplast genomes using Solexa sequencing-by-synthesis technology|journal=[[Nucleic Acids Research]]|date=27 August 2008|volume=36|issue=19|doi=10.1093/nar/gkn502|pages=e122|pmid=18753151|pmc=2577356}}</ref> and is currently regarded as the most widely used platform to replace conventional [[Sanger sequencing]] technique, despite its comparatively low multiplexing capability of samples, as it offers several key advantages: it is automated, quick, highly accurate, capable of sequencing multiple strands simultaneously via [[massive parallel sequencing]], and economically cheaper in case of whole genome sequencing.<ref name=nrg>{{cite journal|last1=Metzker|first1=Michael L.|title=Sequencing technologies – the next generation|journal=[[Nature Reviews Genetics]]|date=8 December 2009|volume=11|issue=1|pages=31–46|doi=10.1038/nrg2626|pmid=19997069|s2cid=205484500}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Pettersson|first1=Erik|last2=Lundeberg|first2=Joakim|last3=Ahmadian|first3=Afshin|title=Generations of sequencing technologies|journal=[[Genomics (journal)|Genomics]]|year=2009|volume=93|issue=2|pages=105–111|doi=10.1016/j.ygeno.2008.10.003|pmid=18992322|doi-access=}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Quail|first1=Michael A|title=A tale of three next generation sequencing platforms: comparison of Ion Torrent, Pacific Biosciences and Illumina MiSeq sequencers|journal=[[BMC Genomics]]|date=24 July 2012|volume=13|issue=341|page=341|doi=10.1186/1471-2164-13-341|pmid=22827831|pmc=3431227 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

He is also known for exploring nanopipette-based (instead of conventional micropipette-based) [[scanning ion-conductance microscopy]] methods.<ref name=BBC /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shevchuk|first1=Andrew I|title=Realizing the biological and biomedical potential of nanoscale imaging using a pipette probe|journal=[[Nanomedicine (Future Medicine journal)|Nanomedicine]]|year=2011|volume=6|issue=3|doi=10.2217/nnm.10.154|pmid=21542692|pages=565–575}}</ref> His research group was successful in achieving very high resolution topographic images of live-cells, in hopping mode imaging, in precise delivery of small molecules to cell, and in studying real time detailed cell-functioning.<ref name="CEN News" /><ref>{{cite journal|title=Scanning Ion Conductance Microscopy|journal=[[Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry]]|year=2012|volume=5|issue=207|pages=207–228|doi=10.1146/annurev-anchem-062011-143203|pmid=22524219|bibcode=2012ARAC....5..207C|last1=Chen|first1=Chiao-Chen|last2=Zhou|first2=Yi|last3=Baker|first3=Lane A.}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Recent advances in high resolution scanning electrochemical microscopy of living cells – A review|journal=[[Analytica Chimica Acta]]|date=2 May 2013|volume=775|doi=10.1016/j.aca.2012.12.042|pmid=23601970|pages=1–13|last1=Bergner|first1=Stefan|last2=Vatsyayan|first2=Preety|last3=Matysik|first3=Frank-Michael|bibcode=2013AcAC..775....1B }}</ref>

Most recently, his group is focusing on 3D [[super-resolution microscopy]] to develop new insights on [[protein misfolding]] and [[Neurodegeneration|neurodegenerative diseases]].<ref name="IOP 2015" />

===Commercial activities===
Klenerman and [[Shankar Balasubramanian]] commercialised their invention on the single-molecule-fluorescence based high-speed DNA sequencing and jointly founded [[Solexa]] in 1998. Later, in 2007, this company was acquired by [[Illumina (company)|Illumina]] for $600&nbsp;million.<ref name="Illumina History" /><ref name=ft>{{cite news|title=Cutting the UK science budget would be a false economy|url=https://www.ft.com/content/9edb5b8c-d75f-11e2-a26a-00144feab7de|access-date=27 January 2016|work=Financial Times|publisher=[[The Nikkei]]|date=18 June 2013}}</ref><ref name=varsity>{{cite news|title=$600m for DNA firm|url=https://www.varsity.co.uk/news/66|access-date=2016-01-27|work=[[Varsity (Cambridge)|Varsity]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Illumina Buys Solexa|url=https://www.forbes.com/2006/11/13/illumina-pharmaceuticals-earnings-markets-equity-cx_rs_1113markets10.html|access-date=27 January 2016|work=[[Forbes]]|date=13 November 2006}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Illumina to Buy Solexa For $600 Million in Stock|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB116343413347821623|access-date=27 January 2016|work=The Wall Street Journal|date=13 November 2006}}</ref>

In 2004, Klenerman co-founded another spin-out company, Ionscope, to supply assembled [[Scanning ion-conductance microscopy|scanning ion-conductance microscopes]] to the research community that looks for high-resolution 3D images of live cells. As per the [[Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council]], as of February 2014, Ionscope sold 35 SICM units worldwide.<ref>{{cite web|title=New microscope technology enables imaging of live cells|url=http://www.bbsrc.ac.uk/research/impact/new-microscope/|publisher=[[BBSRC]]|access-date=30 January 2016}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
The major awards and honours that Klenerman received in recognition of his research work:
* 2007: Awarded [[List of Royal Society of Chemistry medals and awards|RSC Interdisciplinary Award]] by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]].<ref name="RSC Award" /> 
* 2008: Delivered the [[British Biophysical Society]] Lecture at the [[University College Dublin]].<ref>{{cite web|title=British Biophysical Society Lecture Tour|url=https://www.ucd.ie/cscb/main_pages/events/events220408.htm|publisher=[[University College Dublin]]|access-date=27 January 2016}}</ref> 
* 2012: Elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS).<ref name=FRS>{{cite web|title=David Klenerman: Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/david-klenerman-11758/|website=Fellows Directory |publisher=[[Royal Society]]|access-date=2016-01-26}}</ref> 
* 2015: Elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] (FMedSci).<ref name=FMedSci>{{cite web|title=Fellow: Academy of Medical Sciences|url=http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-david-klenerman/|publisher=[[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom]]|access-date=26 January 2016|archive-date=26 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170826031142/https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-david-klenerman}}</ref>
* 2018: Awarded the [[Royal Medal]] by the [[Royal Society]].<ref>[https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/royal-medal/ Royal Medal 2018], Royal society.org. Accessed 30 January 2023.</ref>
* 2019: [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in the [[2019 New Year Honours]] for services to science and the development of high-speed DNA sequencing technology<ref>{{cite web|title=2019 New Year Honours List|url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/768173/NY19_Queens_List__4_.pdf|website=gov.uk|date=31 December 2018}}</ref>
* 2020: Won [[Millennium Technology Prize]] along with Professor Sir Shankar Balasubramanian on their innovation of Next Generation DNA Sequencing
* 2021: Won the 2022 [[Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences]] along with Professor Sir Shankar Balasubramanian and Pascal Mayer on their innovation of Next Generation DNA Sequencing<ref>{{Cite web|title=Breakthrough Prize – Winners Of The 2022 Breakthrough Prizes in Life Sciences, Fundamental Physics And Mathematics Announced|url=https://breakthroughprize.org/News/65|access-date=13 October 2021|website=breakthroughprize.org|language=en}}</ref>
* 2024: [[Canada Gairdner International Award]]<ref>[https://www.gairdner.org/winners Canada Gairdner International Award 2024]</ref>
* 2024: [https://novonordiskfonden.dk/en/prize-recipients/sir-david-klenerman/ Novo Nordisk Prize]
* 2026: [[Princess of Asturias Award]]<ref>[https://www.fpa.es/es/premios-princesa-de-asturias/premiados/2026-david-klenerman-shankar-balasubramanian-y-pascal-mayer/ Princess of Asturias Award 2026]</ref>
* 2026: [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]]<ref>[https://wolffund.org.il/david-klenerman/ Wolf Prize in Chemistry 2026]</ref>
